Pick one installed app and review its permissions, receivers, and risk signals.

Squirrel Detective is a fully offline Android auditor. It enumerates installed packages locally and highlights apps that may silently scan or report on others. No network calls, no analytics.
Sees every app and has internet access

The app declared QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES, which lets it enumerate every installed package, and it also has network access. This combination allows silently sending the list of your apps to a remote server.
Can see the full list of installed apps
QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES bypasses the Android 11+ visibility filter and lets the app see every installed package.
Reads system logs and has internet
READ_LOGS exposes logcat, which can reveal which apps run, what intents are dispatched, and various debug data. Apps on non-rooted devices typically should not require it.
PACKAGE_USAGE_STATS reveals which apps you opened and for how long. Used by parental control and digital wellbeing tools, but also for surveillance.
REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES lets the app install APK files outside Google Play. Legitimate for alternative stores but risky elsewhere — can deliver adware or malicious APKs.
GET_ACCOUNTS returns the list of accounts (Google, mail, etc). Together with internet access, it can be used for de-anonymization.

The app contains a service protected by BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE. Once you turn it on in Accessibility settings, it can read the contents of any screen and emulate gestures. This is the most powerful surveillance channel on Android — turn it on only for trusted apps.
A receiver for ACTION_PACKAGE_ADDED is declared in the manifest. The app gets notified every time you install something.
A receiver for ACTION_PACKAGE_REMOVED is declared in the manifest — the app knows when other packages are uninstalled.
Scans packages right after device boot
The app listens to BOOT_COMPLETED and also has permissions to read the package list or usage history. This is a typical signal of automatic scanning every time the phone is turned on.
SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW lets the app render UI on top of any other app — used for legitimate floating widgets, but also for tap-jacking and phishing overlays.
RECORD_AUDIO with INTERNET means the app can capture audio and send it to a remote server. Required by voice messengers, but suspicious otherwise.
CAMERA with INTERNET means photos and video can be captured and uploaded silently.
SMS access lets the app intercept verification codes and personal messages. Modern Android only allows this for the default SMS app — otherwise it is a strong red flag.
READ_CONTACTS with INTERNET allows the contact book to be uploaded silently.
READ_CALL_LOG / WRITE_CALL_LOG let the app see who you call and when. Restricted to dialer apps in modern Android — otherwise suspicious.
READ_PHONE_STATE / READ_PHONE_NUMBERS expose IMEI, SIM serial, line numbers — used for fingerprinting devices.
ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION or ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION with internet access lets the app track your movements continuously.

The app contains a receiver protected by BIND_DEVICE_ADMIN. Once you activate it as a device admin, it can lock the screen, enforce a password policy, and on older Android versions even wipe the device. Legitimate for MDM only.

The app contains a service protected by BIND_NOTIFICATION_LISTENER_SERVICE. Once you grant it notification access, it sees every notification, including sensitive ones from banking apps and messengers.
The app contains a service protected by BIND_VPN_SERVICE. Once you start its VPN, all device traffic goes through this app — it can inspect or modify everything you send.
The app contains a service protected by BIND_INPUT_METHOD. Once you enable it as a keyboard, it can capture every key you type. Only enable keyboards from trusted sources.
MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE grants read/write access to the entire shared storage — including private app folders on older Android.
WRITE_SECURE_SETTINGS / WRITE_SETTINGS allow changing system-wide configuration including security flags.
GET_TASKS / REAL_GET_TASKS reveal which apps are running. Deprecated, allowed only for system apps — flagged for non-system declarations.
The app was sideloaded (no installer package or unknown installer) and combines several risky permissions. Sideloaded apps with broad access deserve manual review.
The app ships with android:debuggable=true. Production apps should not be debuggable — a debugger can inspect memory and inject code.
The app targets an old SDK level (below API 23). On modern Android this skips the runtime permission model — all dangerous permissions are granted on install without prompt.
The app does not declare a launcher activity, so it has no icon in the app drawer. Combined with sensitive permissions this is a typical pattern for stalkerware.
Plain-language reference for what each Android permission actually grants. No need to google.
A short, human reference for what each Android permission allows. Tap a category to expand.
Lets the app open network connections. Almost universal — but combined with permissions that read your data (contacts, files, location, package list) it is what allows that data to leave the device.

Bypasses the Android 11+ package visibility filter and reveals every installed app on the device. Legitimate for launchers, stores, antivirus and file managers — suspicious anywhere else, especially with INTERNET.
Shows which apps you opened, when, and for how long. Used by digital wellbeing, parental control and stat trackers — also a common stalkerware signal. Must be granted manually in system settings.

Reads the system logcat, where every app prints debug info, intents and crashes. On non-rooted devices Android only grants this to system or developer-mode apps. Anywhere else it is a strong red flag.
Lists currently running tasks and recent activities. Deprecated since Android 5 and reserved for system apps — third-party apps that still declare it look outdated or invasive.

Lets the app read every screen, every text field, and emulate taps and gestures. The most powerful surveillance channel on Android. Grant it only to tools you fully trust (screen readers, password managers).
Device-administrator access can lock the screen, force a password policy, disable the camera and on older Android even wipe the device. Legitimate only for MDM and corporate device management.

Reads every notification posted by every app, including SMS codes, banking alerts and chat previews. Legitimate for smartwatches and notification managers; everywhere else it is a high-risk capability.
Routes the entire device traffic through this app. A malicious or sloppy VPN can inspect, log or modify everything you send. Use only well-known providers.
Lets the app act as a system keyboard, which means it sees every key you type — including passwords. Install only well-known keyboards.
Draws UI on top of every other app. Useful for chat heads and floating widgets — also used for tap-jacking attacks and phishing overlays.
Direct access to the device cameras. Combined with INTERNET it allows photos and video to be uploaded silently. Legitimate camera, video chat and AR apps need it; granted at runtime.

Direct microphone access. With INTERNET it can be used to capture and upload audio. Legitimate for voice messengers, recorders and assistants. Android 12+ shows a status-bar dot whenever the mic is active.
Reads or intercepts SMS messages, including verification codes. Modern Android only gives the full set to the default SMS app — anywhere else this is a serious warning.
Reads or modifies your address book. With INTERNET the contact list can be uploaded silently — a classic data-collection pattern.
Reads or modifies the call history. Restricted to dialer / default phone apps in modern Android. Anywhere else it is suspicious.
Exposes IMEI, SIM serial and the line phone number — used for fingerprinting and de-anonymisation across app reinstalls.
FINE gives precise GPS coordinates, COARSE gives city-block accuracy. Required by maps, navigation and weather apps. With INTERNET they enable continuous tracking.
Continues reading location while the app is in the background. Granted in a separate consent screen — only sensible for navigation, fitness and family-tracking apps.
Read and write the entire shared storage and most app folders. A power-user permission for file managers, backup tools and archivers; risky elsewhere.
Legacy permissions to read or write the public storage (Photos, Downloads, Music). Replaced on Android 13+ by scoped photo / video / audio permissions.
Lets the app install APK files outside Google Play. Required by alternative stores and updaters. Risky in random apps — can deliver adware or malicious updates.
Lists accounts registered on the device (Google, mail, messengers). Together with INTERNET it can be used to identify the user across apps.
Modifies system settings; the SECURE variant can change security-relevant flags. The secure form is reserved for system apps — its presence in a third-party app is a major warning.
Required since Android 13 to show any notifications. Routine for chat, news and email apps — not sensitive on its own.
Lets the app start automatically after the device reboots. Routine for messengers and alarms; combined with package-list or usage-stats access it is a typical sign of background scanning.
Allows long-running background work with a persistent notification — used for music players, navigation, fitness tracking and file uploads. Required by Android, not dangerous on its own.
Keeps the CPU or screen awake. Used by media players, alarms and downloads. Battery-relevant but not a privacy concern.
This is a launcher. It must enumerate installed apps to draw the home screen, so QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES is normal in this context.
This is an app store. Managing installs and updates is its core function, so it has the corresponding permissions.
File managers list APK files and let you install them, so they need package visibility.
Antivirus apps scan every installed package — this is their primary function.
